entry.evidence: We argue that each type of human activity might have a different “temporal signature” (i.e., a characteristic temporal behavior) due to its intrinsic properties.

sequences.source_document: Publisher full text from XML (jats_text), checked against the published PDF

steps.action: The authors identify a gap: freshwater salinization studies are short-term or snapshot, so its temporal dynamics have been overlooked.
steps.quote: Thus, the temporal dynamics of FS have been largely overlooked.

steps.action: The authors propose that each human activity leaves a characteristic temporal signature in river salinity.
steps.quote: each type of human activity might have a different “temporal signature”

steps.action: From published studies the authors derive the expected timing of salinity peaks for agriculture, mining, road de-icing and wastewater.
steps.quote: Therefore, peaks in conductivity are most likely to occur during planting periods, when fertilizer addition and irrigation are maximum.

steps.action: The authors state the aim: to analyse how human activities disrupt the temporal dynamics of EC in Spanish rivers with long, high-resolution data.
steps.quote: The aim of this study was to analyze how human activities might disrupt the temporal dynamics of electrical conductivity

steps.action: The authors hypothesize that low-pressure rivers have low, constant EC and high-pressure rivers have high, variable EC.
steps.quote: We hypothesized that rivers under low human pressure would have low and constant ECs

steps.action: The authors state four driver-specific expectations (I–IV): agricultural peaks in the growing season, mining peaks in heavy rain, road-salt peaks in spring, wastewater maxima in summer.
steps.quote: (II) mining, leading to high ECs near mine tailings during heavy rainfall events

steps.action: The authors choose 13 catchments that span gradients of relief, geology, size, climate and hydrology as found conditions.
steps.quote: We studied 13 river catchments covering a wide range of land reliefs

steps.action: The authors take daily EC for 2007–2011 from 91 stations of the national SAICA monitoring network and compute 24 conductivity indices adapted from hydrological alteration indices.
steps.quote: We used daily measures of electrical conductivity (EC) for the period 2007–2011 from 91 stations

steps.action: The authors compile 14 driver variables: they compute distance to mines and to icy roads in GIS, and take the remaining variables from the coauthors' earlier work (Estévez et al. 2019).
steps.quote: Distance to the nearest mine (P_DMN) and distance to the nearest icy road (P_DIR) were computed in R

steps.action: The authors fit an overall trend in mean EC and estimate a decrease of 17 µS/cm per year.
steps.quote: we found a strong decrease in mean EC (R2 = 0.001; P value < 0.001) at a rate of 17 µS/cm per year

steps.action: After removing collinear indices (VIF > 5), the authors use PCA and clustering to sort the stations into four groups (SCI1–SCI4) along a gradient of EC variability.
steps.quote: the cluster analysis resulted in four groups of stations (SCI1, SCI2, SCI3, and SCI4; Fig. 2)

steps.action: The authors check the PCA ordering with group mean and SD time series (Fig. 3) and with pairwise GAM smooth comparisons, which separate SCI1 from the other groups.
steps.quote: In agreement with the PCA analysis, SCI1 showed the highest EC variations, followed by SCI4, SCI3, and SCI2.

steps.action: The authors fit Random Forests and estimate the relative importance of each driver for EC variation within each group.
steps.quote: According to the Random Forest (R2 = 0.52), the temporal variation in EC was mainly driven by [...] )

steps.action: With ANOVA and Tukey tests the authors compare drivers between groups and find that the most variable group (SCI1) carries the highest human pressure.
steps.quote: SCI1 was the most subjected to human activities, with the highest values of agricultural land, mining, and urban areas

steps.action: The authors exclude geology as the main control: it has low RF importance, and EC does not differ between calcareous and siliceous catchments.
steps.quote: there was no evidence (P value = 0.738) for differences in EC between calcareous

steps.action: The authors regress EC on precipitation by month and by group, and on heavy and low rainfall events, and find month-specific relationships that differ between groups.
steps.quote: We found strong positive linear relationships between precipitation and EC

steps.action: The authors keep the main hypothesis: human activities amplify the temporal variability of EC.
steps.quote: Overall, we found strong evidence for an amplification of the temporal variability in EC in Spanish rivers due to human activities.

steps.action: The authors reject their temporal-signature hypothesis, because the groups do not correspond to single human drivers.
steps.quote: Contrary to our expectations, we found that the grouping of sites according to the temporal variability in EC did not respond to unique human drivers

steps.action: The authors revise the account to a combination of drivers and attribute the mismatch to regional differences in crops and hydrology.
steps.quote: This is likely related with regional differences in the human drivers of FS

steps.action: The authors check that their EC values fall within the ranges reported by earlier studies of Spanish rivers (Table S5).
steps.quote: the range of EC values reported in our study matches those reported by previous studies in Spanish rivers

steps.action: Citing others' work, the authors propose that the decreasing EC trend reflects improved and more numerous wastewater treatment plants.
steps.quote: These EC trends could be linked to technology improvements and the increase in the number of wastewater treatment plants

steps.action: The authors compare the dominance of agriculture with global and Spanish studies that name agriculture as the main driver of freshwater salinization.
steps.quote: This is in alignment with previous studies at the global

steps.action: The authors keep the sub-claim that agriculture disrupts the temporal dynamics of salinity, not only its level.
steps.quote: Our study reveals that agriculture is not only increasing the salt concentration of rivers, but also disrupting the natural temporal dynamics of salinity.

steps.action: From the group-specific precipitation months, the authors propose that human and climatic drivers interact, with mechanisms for each group (soil salt build-up, road salt, mine tailings flushed in autumn rain).
steps.quote: suggests that human activities and climatic drivers interact to modulate the temporal dynamics of salt pollution

steps.action: The authors set the proposed mechanisms against cited local studies: irrigation-driven EC rise in the Cidacos River and roadside soil salinization near the Aragon, Araquil and Arga rivers.
steps.quote: Concordantly, Merchant et al. (75) found that EC significantly increased in the Cidacos river

steps.action: The authors check the road-salt interpretation within SCI2: rivers near snow-affected roads have higher mean EC and SD than the rest of the group.
steps.quote: Concordantly, in our study, these rivers showed higher mean and standard deviation EC (670 ± 155 µS/cm) than the rest of the rivers

steps.action: The authors restrict the claim's range: the rivers studied are large and dilute salt, so effects in small streams may be larger.
steps.quote: Thus, our results need to be taken with caution

steps.action: The authors conclude that human activities disrupted EC dynamics in 2007–2011, through a combination of drivers led by agriculture.
steps.quote: [...] evidence for a disruption of the temporal dynamics of EC due to human activities during the period study (2007–2011).

tree.answer: Temporal variability of river EC under human pressure; groups of rivers with distinct EC variability are established by clustering
EC is measured directly at monitoring stations; driver effects are not observed and are inferred statistically
Analyse how human activities disrupt the temporal dynamics of EC
Rivals: driver-specific temporal signatures (agriculture, mining, road salt, wastewater) versus natural controls (geology, precipitation)
Distinct seasonal timing of EC peaks is predicted for each driver, but the timing is not tested driver by driver
Found: a natural gradient across 91 stations in 13 catchments, with archival monitoring data

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats across 91 stations and five years of daily data
Limited: a second method agrees with the PCA ordering (Fig. 3, GAMs); one within-group check; no sensitivity tests
Human amplification of EC variability kept as best explanation; temporal-signature hypothesis and geology control rejected

end.claim: Human activities, mainly agriculture combined with road de-icing, mining and wastewater, amplify the temporal variability of EC in Spanish rivers, with no driver-specific temporal signature.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the drivers of the clustered EC-variability groups showed that the most variable group carries the highest human pressure, and the attribution rests on this comparison.

gates.evidence: The EC data are archival SAICA monitoring data, and the driver variables come from GIS or the coauthors' earlier work, so no hypothesis directed acquisition. The temporal-signature expectation could fail and did fail (§4 ¶1), but the main amplification claim rests on correlational group comparisons with no control for natural variability, so its test was weak. No pre-registration is reported; the hypotheses appear in the Introduction and cannot be dated relative to the analysis.

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: agriculture as main driver of EC variability, best_explanation; month-specific EC–precipitation relations, regularity_in_range (Table S4 R² only in the supplement); overall EC decrease of 17 µS/cm per year, estimate_with_resolution without a reported uncertainty, and called 'strong' despite R² = 0.001; the temporal-signature hypothesis and geology as main control are excluded. A single Random Forest R² (0.52) is reported, not per group. Most driver variables were inherited from Estévez et al. 2019 (coauthors). Expectations I–IV are not tested one by one against the timing indices (JMax, JMin); the discussion maps them onto groups only post hoc (inference). There are no sensitivity tests for clustering choices, the number of clusters, the VIF threshold, the snow-day threshold for icy roads, or the subset of mine types. GAM diagnostics are said to be run but are not reported. The axis 'Days' (0–125) in Fig. 3 is not explained. No review file or earlier version was supplied, so the review history is unknown. Composition coded natures_repetition because conditions are found and repeated across stations with fitted relations; trace_series would also fit the best-explanation status (inference).

disagreements.target: Prior freshwater salinization research based on short-term laboratory or mesocosm experiments and snapshot field studies
disagreements.support: The authors argue that daily multi-year monitoring data are needed to capture temporal dynamics that snapshot designs miss.
disagreements.quote: The vast majority of studies on FS have focused on short-term laboratory or mesocosm experiments, or on snap-shot field studies

disagreements.target: The general view that freshwater ecosystems are getting saltier (Kaushal et al. 2005; Dugan et al. 2017)
disagreements.support: Mean EC across the 91 Spanish rivers decreased from 2007 to 2011, which the authors set against the global salinization trend.
disagreements.quote: it is important to notice that many freshwater ecosystems are getting saltier

disagreements.target: Road salt pollution research focused almost exclusively on Canada and the US (Cunillera-Montcusí et al. 2022)
disagreements.support: ANOVA shows strong differences in icy-road proximity between groups, and the Random Forest ranks this variable highly in SCI1 and SCI2.
disagreements.quote: So far, road salt pollution of rivers and streams has been almost exclusively studied in Canada and the US

disagreements.target: Geology as the main driver of salinity changes (Meybeck 2003)
disagreements.support: Geology has low Random Forest importance, and EC does not differ between calcareous and siliceous catchments, so human activities appear to override geology.
disagreements.quote: This suggests that human activities are overriding the influence of geology, which is the main driver of changes in salinity in pristine rivers

alternatives_considered.reason: Low Random Forest importance and no evidence of an EC difference between rock types (P = 0.738)
